His opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro, fled the country following his loss amid an ongoing corruption investigation. All the ballots from Tuesday’s Israeli election have been counted, and there’s still no clear winning coalition. On Thursday, Israel’s Central Election Committee said Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc holds 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while opposition parties have 67. And Vice President J.D. Vance reportedly sent a letter to a senior Iranian official in Tehran aimed at reviving peace talks to end the Iran war. But when Donald Trump was asked if he directed Vance to revive peace talks, he claimed the letter was about medical supplies.

items.title: New economic data challenges Fed chief’s not-too-hot perspective By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - New data may challenge Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh’s sense that the US economy can handle a robust expansion without stoking inflation, as a key measure of price pressures jumped and strong consumer spending and business investment pushed growth further beyond the level most central bank officials see as sustainable. ... The jump in third-quarter gross domestic product, announced on Thursday by the US Commerce Department, however, was even faster than anticipated, with output growing at a 3.4% annualized rate in the July-September period, consumer spending rising by a robust 3.8%, and investment in business equipment up a massive 20.9%. The pace may not continue. Consumer spending, for example, grew faster than income in the recent GDP report, a situation some economists said was unlikely to last, and Warsh said on Wednesday that a recent tightening in credit markets showed investors had become "more discerning in ... But the data in hand still show an economy that so far has not slowed despite the outlook for tighter monetary policy, with strong demand now coinciding with broad-based inflation. Different measures of inflation’s breadth show anywhere from roughly 50% to nearly 60% of the items in the Personal Consumption Expenditures Price Index, the gauge the Fed uses for its 2% inflation target, posting annual price increases of more than 3% in September — far above pre-COVID-19 norms for a measure Warsh said he sees as a good indicator of underlying inflation trends. Though the number of items above that 3% level fell slightly last month, Diane Swonk, chief economist at KPMG, said the details of the PCE report showed inflation was broadly persistent across the economy, particularly in service industries where Fed rate hikes may have less of an impact.

items.title: PCE inflation report September 2026:
items.excerpt: The pace of price increases stepped up in September, keeping inflation well above the Federal Reserve's target, while the economy grew faster than expected in the third quarter, according to Commerce Department reports Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures price index increased a seasonally adjusted 0.5% for the month, putting the annual inflation rate at 3.6%. The monthly increase was the largest since March but in line with the Dow Jones consensus, while the annual rate was 0.1 percentage point below. Excluding food and energy, the core PCE posted respective readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, in line with the consensus. While the Fed follows both measures closely, officials generally see the core reading as more indicative of longer-term inflation trends. While inflation continued to run ahead of the Fed's 2% target, the Commerce Department also reported that gross domestic product was strong in the third quarter. GDP increased at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, better than the 3.1% estimate and well ahead of the 2.2% in the second quarter. Also, in September consumer spending proved resilient, climbing 0.5%, a bit below the forecast for a 0.6% gain, while personal income rose 0.2%, compared with the estimate for 0.3%. ... There was some good inflation news for the period: On a quarterly basis, PCE prices rose 2.1% on the headline number and 2.5% for core, down respectively from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter. September's price increases were driven largely by a surge in energy costs that economists fear could be spreading to other parts of the economy. Gasoline and other energy goods saw a 9.2% rise for the month while energy goods and services broadly jumped 5.4%. At the same time, services prices excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs increased 0.3%.

items.title: St. Louis Fed's Musalem: Another rate hike needed 'soon'
items.excerpt: St. Louis Federal Reserve President Alberto Musalem said Friday that higher interest rates will be needed in the near future to rein in inflation. "I judge that additional firming of monetary policy will be necessary, and soon," Musalem said in prepared remarks for the Shadow Open Market Committee, a gathering of economists focused on the central bank. Musalem's comments offer the first morsels of insight into what leaders at the Fed see next following Wednesday's decision to hold interest rates steady. It will also bolster the view among investors that the Fed will return to hiking rates at its next meeting in December. Fed funds futures traders are pricing in a roughly 76% likelihood of the Fed lifting rates by a quarter percentage point at that gathering, according to CME's FedWatch tool. "Incremental adjustments made earlier are usually less disruptive than larger and abrupt actions taken later," Musalem said. "Moving sooner in smaller steps while inflation expectations are anchored has a better chance of succeeding without adverse impact on the labor market or economic growth." ... But Musalem warned that inflation is "too high," citing the personal consumption expenditures price index released Thursday that showed annual inflation above 3%. Fed officials have been closely monitoring inflation expectations among consumers and investors to ensure they don't get too far above the central bank's long-term target of 2%. He said there's a likely scenario where inflation remains above 2% into the future unless the Fed adjusts monetary policy. "The best that monetary policy can do now for employment and economic growth is to restore price stability in a timely manner," Musalem said.

items.title: U.S. Inflation Accelerates to 3.7% as Gasoline Prices Jump | EconoTimes
items.excerpt: U.S. inflation accelerated in September as gasoline prices climbed, while research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York points to a separate tariff-related pressure on consumer-goods costs. The Consumer Price Index (CPI), reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), rose 0.6% from August on a seasonally adjusted basis and 3.7% over 12 months, up from 3.4% in August. Gasoline prices increased 9.1% during the month, and the gasoline index was 34.2% higher than a year earlier. Food at home fell 0.1% for the month and rose 1.8% over the year. The Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) reported that its personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index advanced 0.5% in September and 3.6% from a year earlier. Excluding food and energy, the index rose 0.3% for the month and 3.1% over 12 months. Neither release calculated tariffs’ contribution to overall inflation; the BLS said gasoline contributed more than half of September’s monthly CPI increase. In the New York Fed researchers’ model, a one-point rise in the average tariff rate corresponds to an estimated 0.25% increase in consumer-goods prices after 12 months. The researchers found that most tariff costs passed through to U.S. import prices. The researchers said higher costs for imported inputs can feed into retail prices through U.S. producers.

items.title: Trump escalates legal challenges, scrambles schedule as US midterm elections near By Reuters
items.excerpt: Published Oct 30, 2026, 06:11 AM Updated Oct 30, 2026, 02:49 PM ... By Andrew Goudsward and Jarrett Renshaw WASHINGTON, Oct 30 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump on Friday intensified his effort to save Republicans’ congressional majorities ahead of Tuesday’s US midterm election, restoring planned 11th-hour rallies he had canceled a day earlier while stepping up legal interventions that could pave the way for court challenges to the results. The November 3 contest has already drawn 48 million early ballots, more than any other midterm election in US history, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, with even the American-born Pope Leo casting a ballot by mail. Trump’s fellow Republicans are likely to lose their slim majority in the US House of Representatives, according to nonpartisan analysts, with control of the Senate expected to be hard fought. The Trump administration pushed forward in legal cases in Alaska, home to a Senate contest that may play a pivotal role in determining the majority, and California, which historically takes more time than most other states in counting ballots. The Justice Department filed an amended lawsuit in Alaska on Thursday seeking to block the certification of results in the event of a narrow Republican loss, citing a New York Times report that Democratic operatives recruited a spoiler candidate with the same name as the Republican incumbent. The FBI was expected to hold a press conference on Friday at the US Attorney’s office in Anchorage, an agency spokesperson confirmed. In California, meanwhile, the Justice Department is escalating its pressure campaign against state election officials, issuing subpoenas as part of a criminal probe into alleged voting by non-citizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters. Taken together, the moves are an extraordinary federal intervention in state-run elections, which are administered locally under the US Constitution. Election officials around the country have told ⁠Reuters they are bracing for further legal challenges from Washington. Trump has long sought to sow distrust of election results, falsely claiming for years that his 2020 election loss to Democrat Joe Biden was the result of widespread fraud. Voter fraud in the US is extremely rare, studies and investigations have found. ... TRUMP’S CANCELED RALLIES BACK ON The dispute in Alaska, home to one of about 10 highly competitive Senate races, could leave control of the chamber unclear for weeks. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the majority from Republicans. If Democrats take one or both chambers of Congress, they intend to launch investigations into Trump’s administration and increase pressure on the president to end the war against Iran. On Friday, Trump will campaign in Florida, the latest in a series of rallies he has headlined in states he won handily in 2024 but where Democrats are unexpectedly competitive. Earlier this week, Trump campaigned in deep-red Mississippi and South Carolina, and the White House said on Friday that the president would hold weekend rallies in Kansas and Iowa, less than 24 hours after they had been called off. Trump won all four states by anywhere from 13 to 22 percentage points two years ago. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, whom Trump defeated in the 2024 election, will rally for Democrats in Atlanta on Friday. ALASKA SENATE DISPUTE In its revised lawsuit in Alaska on Thursday, the Justice Department wrote that operatives for Democratic candidate Mary Peltola orchestrated a "sham campaign for the purpose of misleading Alaskan voters." The New York Times reported on Wednesday that the operatives convinced a retired teacher living in a remote fishing village named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. to appear on the ballot alongside the Republican incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan. Peltola’s campaign asked a judge to dismiss the Justice Department’s updated lawsuit, arguing it has no legal basis. The campaign has previously said it had "no involvement with either Sullivan campaign." The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee has denied involvement and accused Republicans of propping up third-party candidates of their own in other races. Daniel J. Sullivan, listed on the ballot as unaffiliated with any party, has previously denied that his aim was to cause confusion or divert votes from Dan S. Sullivan. In California, meanwhile, the Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder’s office received grand jury subpoenas last week in the Justice Department’s investigation into alleged non-citizen voting. "At every step, the US Department ​of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach," Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said in a statement ​on Thursday.
